extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in real analysis/measure theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of measurable sets/functions, construction and basic properties of the Lebesgue integral, key convergence theorems, and the extension theorem for measures. Targets learning to define, approximate, and integrate measurable functions and to extend measures from rings to σ-rings/σ-algebras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of measurable function (inverse-image characterizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → R* is measurable if f^{-1}((−∞,c)) is measurable for every real number c. Equivalently one may require f^{-1}((−∞,c]), f^{-1}((c, +∞]), or f^{-1}([c, +∞]) to be measurable for every c; the implications (i)⇒(ii)⇒(iii)⇒(iv)⇒(i) follow from listed set-identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives four equivalent inverse-image criteria (labeled (i)–(iv)) and shows how they imply one another via identities involving countable unions/intersections. Use any of these forms when checking measurability; manipulations with inverse images are standard (see Appendix A reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and situational criteria for measurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Special-case observations: with the trivial σ-algebra {∅,X} only constant functions are measurable; with the full power set every function to R* is measurable; continuous functions on R are Borel measurable; functions that are continuous except at countably many points are Borel measurable; every Borel measurable function is Lebesgue measurable, and Riemann integrable functions (extended by 0 off their domain) are Lebesgue measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several concrete examples are given to show when measurability is automatic or fails. The text points out an exercise (Problem 33) showing some Riemann integrable functions need not be Borel measurable, and explains how continuity plus countable exceptional sets yields Borel measurability by restricting inverse images to unions of intervals and countable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic closure properties of measurable functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant functions are measurable; if f is measurable then the inverse image of any interval or any open set in R* is measurable; the positive and negative parts f^+, f^-, and |f| are measurable (Proposition 5.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs rely on representing intervals as unions/intersections of sets of the kind in the measurability definition and using closure of the σ-algebra under countable unions/intersections. The page explicitly treats f^+, f^- and related identities (e.g. |f| = f^+ + f^-) and handles boundary cases (c < 0 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure under arithmetic operations and scalar multiples
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are measurable and a∈R, then a f is measurable; f+g and f g are measurable provided the sum and product are everywhere defined in R* (Proposition 5.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses rational approximations: represent sets {x: f+g > c} as countable unions/intersections involving rationals to reduce to inverse images for f and g. For product, special-case checks and decompositions into nonnegative parts (f^+, f^-) are used to handle sign issues. The text notes multiplication in R* defines 0·(±∞)=0 by convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure under sup, inf, limsup, liminf, and pointwise limits
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sequence {f_n} of measurable functions, sup_n f_n, inf_n f_n, lim sup_n f_n, and lim inf_n f_n are measurable (Proposition 5.8). If f_n→f pointwise in R*, then f is measurable (Corollary 5.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce these operations to countable unions/intersections of inverse-image sets already known to be measurable. Corollary 5.9 specializes to finite maxima/minima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple functions: canonical expansion and measurability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple function s : X → R* has a finite image and admits a canonical expansion s = Σ_{n=1}^N c_n I_{E_n} where c_n are distinct reals and E_n are disjoint nonempty sets unioning X. s is measurable iff all sets E_n in the canonical expansion are measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The canonical expansion is unique and the page emphasizes that s^{-1}((c, +∞]) etc. are unions of the E_n and thus measurability reduces to measurability of those atoms. Subsequent lemmas (5.12–5.14) develop integrals and inequalities for simple functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation of nonnegative functions by increasing measurable simple functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For any function f : X → [0, +∞], there exists a sequence {s_n} of simple functions with 0 ≤ s_n ≤ s_{n+1} and s_n(x) ↑ f(x) for all x. If f is measurable, the s_n may be taken measurable (Proposition 5.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives an explicit dyadic-style construction (partitioning ranges into intervals [j/2^n, (j+1)/2^n)) producing measurable simple approximants. This is the standard tool for defining ∫f by approximating from below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator function measurability equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The indicator function I_E of a set E is measurable iff E is measurable (because (I_E)^{-1}((c,+∞]) is ∅, E, or X depending on c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation is used repeatedly to move between set-measure statements and function-integral statements (indicator functions are the building blocks for simple functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Lebesgue integral for nonnegative measurable functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If s is a nonnegative measurable simple function with canonical expansion s = Σ c_n I_{A_n}, define ∫_E s dµ = Σ c_n µ(A_n ∩ E). For a nonnegative measurable f, define ∫_E f dµ = sup{∫_E s dµ : 0 ≤ s ≤ f, s simple} (section opening of Lebesgue integral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition uses approximations from below by simple functions and yields a value in R* (possibly +∞). For f ≡ 0 the integral is 0. Examples show consistency with counting measure and Riemann integrals for continuous functions on bounded intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Lebesgue integral for general measurable functions and integrability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a measurable f, set f^+, f^- as usual and define ∫_E f dµ = ∫_E f^+ dµ − ∫_E f^- dµ provided these two integrals are not both infinite. f is integrable on E iff ∫_E f^+ dµ and ∫_E f^- dµ are both finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains this is consistent with the nonnegative case, and shows that when f is integrable the sets where f^+ or f^- are infinite must have measure zero. Integrability is equivalent to finiteness of ∫ |f| dµ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of the integral (monotonicity, additivity, constants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 5.15 enumerates properties: (a) If f≥0 and µ(E)=0 then ∫_E f dµ = 0; (b) If F⊆E and f≥0 then ∫_F f dµ ≤ ∫_E f dµ and consequences for differences; (c) If c is constant in R* then ∫_E c dµ = c µ(E); (d) scaling by constants: ∫_E c f dµ = c ∫_E f dµ where defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce to the simple-function case and use additivity and monotonicity of µ. The text handles infinite constants and sign cases by decomposition into positive/negative parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and localization of the integral (inequality under pointwise ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are measurable, their integrals over E are defined, and f(x) ≤ g(x) on E, then ∫_E f dµ ≤ ∫_E g dµ (Proposition 5.16). Localization: inequalities need hold only on E even though functions are defined on all X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses simple-function approximations and decompositions into positive/negative parts; the remark emphasizes this locality property is convenient in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete additivity of the set function E ↦ ∫_E f dµ when ∫_X f dµ defined
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is measurable and ∫_X f dµ is defined (i.e., not of form ∞−∞), then the set function ρ(E)=∫_E f dµ is completely additive: for any disjoint sequence {E_n}, ρ(⋃ E_n)=Σ ρ(E_n) (Theorem 5.19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: prove for nonnegative f first, reduce to simple functions and use complete additivity of µ; then extend to general f by splitting into f^+ and f^- when integrals are not both infinite. This fact is used repeatedly (e.g., in proofs of convergence theorems and linearity for unbounded functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {f_n} is an increasing sequence of measurable functions on E with f_n(x) ↑ f(x) (pointwise, limit in R*), then ∫_E f_n dµ ↑ ∫_E f dµ; equivalently lim_n ∫_E f_n dµ = ∫_E f dµ (Theorem 5.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses this generalizes counting-measure monotone results and that one may use a single increasing approximating sequence of simple functions to compute ∫. The proof constructs sets where cs(x) < f_n(x) eventually and uses complete additivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity/additivity of integration for possibly unbounded functions (complete-additivity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are measurable, their sum h=f+g is everywhere defined, and ∫_E f dµ and ∫_E g dµ are defined, then ∫_E h dµ is defined and equals ∫_E f dµ + ∫_E g dµ (Proposition 5.26). Complete additivity of µ is used in the unbounded case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof treats simple functions first, then approximates general nonnegative parts by increasing simple sequences and applies MCT. The text remarks that complete additivity is not needed when functions are bounded (uniform approximation), but is essential in the unbounded case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries: dominated integrability, small-measure control, and almost-everywhere notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Various corollaries: if |f|≤g a.e. with g integrable then f integrable and |∫ f| ≤ ∫ |f| ≤ ∫ g (Corollary 5.21/DCT special case); if f∈L^1 then for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 so that µ(E)≤δ ⇒ ∫_E |f| dµ ≤ ε (Corollary 5.24); if f=0 on a set of full measure then ∫ f=0 and conversely ∫ f=0 for nonnegative f implies f=0 a.e. (Corollary 5.23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard useful consequences for manipulating integrals: control of integrals on small measure sets, equivalence of integrals on sets differing by null sets, and definitions/terminology for 'almost everywhere'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatou’s Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sequence {f_n} of nonnegative measurable functions on E, ∫_E (lim inf_n f_n) dµ ≤ lim inf_n ∫_E f_n dµ (Theorem 5.29). In particular, if f_n→f pointwise then ∫ f ≤ lim inf ∫ f_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to monotone convergence by setting g_n = inf_{k≥n} f_k and letting g_n↑ lim inf f_n, then apply MCT. The text points out Fatou applies to earlier counterexamples where interchange of limit and integral fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {f_n} are measurable on E and f_n→f pointwise, and there exists an integrable g with |f_n| ≤ g for all n, then ∫_E f_n dµ → ∫_E f dµ and f is integrable (Theorem 5.30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Fatou applied to g ± f_n to obtain inequalities yielding convergence of integrals. The text reduces to the case g finite a.e. by altering functions on null sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension Theorem for measures under σ-finiteness (existence and uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 5.5 (Extension Theorem) stated: let A be a ring of subsets of a nonempty set X and ∫ be a nonnegative completely additive set function on A that is σ-finite on A (containing X?). Then ∫ extends uniquely to a measure µ on the smallest σ-ring (or σ-algebra) containing A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The following section outlines the classic Carathéodory-style extension idea: define outer/inner approximations µ^*(U) for countable increasing unions and µ_*(K) for countable decreasing intersections, show these match on a σ-algebra containing A, and thereby obtain the extension. σ-finiteness is used to ensure uniqueness/existence in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and properties of upper/lower set approximations (µ^* and µ_*) via countable unions/intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Define classes U = countable unions of sets in A and K = countable intersections of sets in A. For U = ⋃ A_n with A_n∈A, set µ^*(U) = lim ∫(A_n). For K = ⋂ C_n with C_n∈A decreasing, set µ_*(K) = lim ∫(C_n). Lemma 5.32 records: (a) µ^* and µ_* agree with ∫ on A; (b) monotonicity: if U⊆V in U then µ^*(U) ≤ µ^*(V); (c) similar monotonicity for µ_* on K; (d) continuity property: lim µ^*(U_n)=µ^*(⋃U_n) for increasing U_n in U, and lim µ_*(K_n)=µ_*(⋂K_n) for decreasing K_n in K when measures finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma sets up well-defined inner/outer approximations independent of the chosen approximating sequences (use additivity/continuity results). These approximations are the building blocks for showing the class where µ^*=µ_* is a σ-algebra containing A and yields the extension.
